4.7  Equality and Unique Existence

Sections 4.3 to 4.6 gave the four quantifier rules, and with them every logical symbol of the language of Section 4.2 (the connectives, ⊥, the quantifiers, and equality) has rules, except one. So far the equals sign has been treated like a predicate symbol: a=b was an atomic formula like P(a), and no rule looked inside it. Yet almost every calculation in mathematics is a chain of equations, and every use of “the” (the limit, the supremum, the inverse) quietly asserts that something is unique. This section adds the two rules for equality, =I and =E, which say together that equals may be replaced by equals. Its first application is the phrase “there is exactly one”, which is an existential statement together with an equation. The section ends by completing the table of rules, phrases, and Lean tactics that Chapter 1 began.

4.7.1. What the rules so far cannot do with an equation

Here is the first line of a calculation any reader has written:

Since a=b and a+a=2a, we have b+b=2b.

Nothing could be simpler, and nothing in Sections 4.3–4.6 derives it. The line a=b is an atomic formula, and so far the rules have treated = exactly as they treat a two-place predicate symbol written between its terms, like the R in front of R(a,b). From the premises R(a,b) and P(a) no rule gives P(b): a relation between a and b says nothing, by itself, about the properties of either. The quantifier rules do not help either, since neither premise begins with a quantifier. As far as the rules of Chapters 1–2 and Sections 4.3–4.6 are concerned, a=b could mean “a is less than b” or “a and b are coprime”, and under those readings the general pattern behind the step, from R(a,b) and P(a) to P(b), fails: reading R(a,b) as a<b and P(x) as x<1 over Z, with a=0 and b=5, both premises are true and P(b) is false.

What makes the step correct is what = means: a and b are names of the same object. Any statement true of the object is true of it whichever name is used. Two things follow, and they are the two rules of this section.

  1. Every term names the same object as itself. Nothing needs to be assumed to write t=t.
  2. If t1 and t2 name the same object, then a statement about t1 may be rewritten as the same statement about t2.

The first rule is unusual: it cites no earlier line at all. Chapter 1 anticipated this when it defined rules (Section 1.2): the definition of a rule schema (Definition 1.2.1) was worded so that a rule of Chapter 4 could have no given lines at all. This is that rule.

4.7.2. The rules for equality

Everything is equal to itself, and equals may be replaced by equals.

Definition 4.7.1 (Rules for Equality)
kt=t=I
it1=t2
jφ[t1/x]
kφ[t2/x]=E i, j

The rule =I (equality introduction, or reflexivity) writes t=t for any term t, at any line, citing nothing. The rule =E (equality elimination, or substitution of equals) cites an equation t1=t2 on line i and a line j of the form φ[t1/x], both available at line k, and writes φ[t2/x] on line k. Here φ is any formula and x any variable, subject to one side condition: both t1 and t2 are free for x in φ (Definition 4.2.6).

In words: =I says that every term equals itself. =E says that when t1=t2 is known, a line that says something about t1 may be rewritten as the same thing said about t2. The formula φ is the “something”: a statement with a hole x, which line j fills with t1 and line k fills with t2.

Read the definition clause by clause.

  1. =I cites nothing. Its justification is “=I” alone. It is the first primitive rule of the book with no given lines (derived rules from results with no premises, such as LEM of Section 2.5, already cite nothing), and so it may stand anywhere: as the first line of a derivation with no premises, or deep inside a box.
  2. The equation is read from left to right. The cited equation t1=t2 licenses replacing t1 by t2, and not the other way round. From a=b and P(b), the rule does not give P(a), because P(b) is φ[b/x] for φ=P(x), and the equation would have to be b=a. The reverse direction needs one more step, symmetry, which we derive below.
  3. Some or all occurrences. The choice of φ decides which occurrences of t1 are replaced: exactly those that φ marks with x. Occurrences of t1 that φ writes out are left alone. Choosing φ is the whole art of using the rule.
  4. Free for x. Neither term may have a variable captured by a quantifier of φ, the condition of Definition 4.2.6 that the rules of Sections 4.3 and 4.5 also carry. The nonexample below shows what goes wrong without it.

One line, many readings. Take the equation a=b and the line a+a=2⋅a. The term a occurs three times in the line, and φ may mark any of them. Some of the choices:

φ φ[a/x] (the cited line) φ[b/x] (the new line)
x+a=2⋅a a+a=2⋅a b+a=2⋅a
a+x=2⋅a a+a=2⋅a a+b=2⋅a
a+a=2⋅x a+a=2⋅a a+a=2⋅b
x+x=2⋅x a+a=2⋅a b+b=2⋅b
a+a=2⋅a a+a=2⋅a a+a=2⋅a

Each of the three occurrences is marked or not, so there are 23=8 choices in all, and each is a legal step. The fourth row is the step of the opening calculation. The last row is the degenerate choice: φ contains no x, so φ[a/x] and φ[b/x] are both φ, and the rule copies the line unchanged. It is legal and useless, and it shows that “some occurrences” includes “none”. Another degenerate case: the equation may be t=t itself, and then =E again returns the cited line.

Quick check. From the equation x0=3 and the line x0⋅x0>x0, which formula φ makes =E give 3⋅3>x0? Which gives x0⋅3>3?

Solution. For 3⋅3>x0, take φ=(z⋅z>x0), with a variable z that appears nowhere else: φ[x0/z] is the cited line and φ[3/z] is 3⋅3>x0. For x0⋅3>3, take φ=(x0⋅z>z). The hole has to be a variable other than x0, since the occurrences of x0 that stay must be written out in φ.

A nonexample: capture. Take the equation a=y, with y a variable, and the line ∃y(y<a). It is tempting to “substitute y for a” and write ∃y(y<y). With φ=∃y(y<x), the cited line is φ[a/x], and the new line would be φ[y/x]. But y is not free for x in φ: the x sits inside ∃y, and the y put there would be captured. The side condition fails, and rightly. Read over Z, with a and y both naming 0, the premises say “a=y” (true) and “some integer is less than 0” (true), while ∃y(y<y) says that some integer is less than itself (false).

1a=y
2∃y(y<a)
3∃y(y<y)=E 1, 2

Line 3 breaks the side condition of Definition 4.7.1. What the argument meant to say needs a different name for the bound variable: ∃z(z<a), which is the same sentence up to renaming (Section 4.2), becomes ∃z(z<y), which is true when y names 0.

Why these two rules. They are exactly the two facts about “same object” listed above, and nothing else about equality needs to be assumed. Symmetry (s=t gives t=s), transitivity (s=t and t=u give s=u), and “applying the same function to both sides” are all derived below. So the two rules play for = the part that the introduction and elimination rules played for each connective: one builds an equation, one uses it. The name of =E is less natural than the others, since the equation is used to rewrite some other line; but “elimination” fits, since the rule takes an equation apart into its use.

Warning. A bound variable is not a place to substitute. From x=0 and ∀x(x=x), the line ∀x(0=x) does not follow by =E, although it looks like “replace the first x by 0”. The x’s of ∀x(x=x) are bound, and substitution replaces only free occurrences (Definition 4.2.5). To write ∀x(x=x) as φ[x/z], either z does not occur free in φ, and then φ[0/z] is the unchanged line, or z occurs free in φ (for instance, φ is ∀x(z=x)), and then every free z lies inside ∀x, so x is not free for z in φ and the side condition fails. Over Z, with x naming 0, the premises are true and ∀x(0=x) is false.

4.7.3. Symmetry, transitivity and congruence

Everything we expect of equality now follows from the two rules. Each derivation below is short, and the only thought in each is the choice of φ.

It turns out that the equation in =E may be read in either direction after all, at the cost of two extra lines (an =I and an =E; after the abbreviation (sym) below, just one), and that equations chain:

Proposition 4.7.1 (Equality Is Symmetric and Transitive)

For all terms s, t, u:

  • (a) s=t⊢t=s;
  • (b) s=t,t=u⊢s=u.

Idea. For (a), the goal t=s must be the last line of an =E that uses the premise s=t (it is the only equation available), so it has the form φ[t/x], and the cited line φ[s/x] must already be on a line. Try φ=(x=s): then φ[t/x] is t=s, the goal, and φ[s/x] is s=s, which =I supplies for free. For (b), rewrite the t of the first premise using the second: φ=(s=x).

Proof.

  • (a) With φ:=(x=s), for a variable x that occurs in neither s nor t, the line s=s is φ[s/x] and the goal t=s is φ[t/x]. Both terms are free for x in φ, since φ has no quantifier. So the following is a derivation:
    1s=t
    2s=s=I
    3t=s=E 1, 2
  • (b) With φ:=(s=x), for a variable x that does not occur in s, the first premise s=t is φ[t/x] and the goal s=u is φ[u/x]; again φ has no quantifier. So the following is a derivation:
1s=t
2t=u
3s=u=E 2, 1

Line 3 of (b) cites the equation t=u on line 2 as the rule’s line i, and s=t on line 1 as its line j. This proves (a) and (b).

Notice where the “reflexivity” line went in (a): the equation s=t was not rewritten at all. It was the tool, and the line it rewrote, s=s, was manufactured for the purpose. This is the typical use of =I: it supplies a line for =E to work on.

From now on, symmetry and transitivity may be used as one line, with the justifications “(sym)” and “(trans)”: each abbreviates the three-line derivation above with the given terms in place of s, t, u. This is the license of Definition 2.3.1, extended from statement letters to terms. The extension is harmless for the same reason: the derivations above used nothing about s, t, u except that they are terms, so they can be pasted in with any terms.

The next derivation is the rule behind “apply f to both sides”. Let f be a one-place function symbol, and a, b constants.

1a=b
2f(a)=f(a)=I
3f(a)=f(b)=E 1, 2

Here φ=(f(a)=f(x)): it keeps the first a and marks the second. With φ=(f(x)=f(x)) instead, the same two lines would give f(b)=f(b), which is true and useless. Nothing is special about f: the same three lines give a2=b2 from a=b, or a+c=b+c, or |a|=|b|. Every “do the same thing to both sides of an equation” is this derivation.

The last derivation of this group has no premises at all. It says that equals share every property P.

Claim. ⊢∀x∀y(x=y→(P(x)→P(y))).

Finding it. The goal is ∀x, so the search method of Section 2.6, with the step of Section 4.4, opens a flagged box for x0; the new goal ∀y(…) opens a second flagged box, for y0. The goal x0=y0→(P(x0)→P(y0)) is an implication, so a box opens with x0=y0, and the new goal P(x0)→P(y0) opens another, with P(x0). Now the goal is P(y0), the resources are x0=y0 and P(x0), and one =E with φ=P(x) finishes. Every line but one was written by a goal-directed step.

1x0y0x0=y0
2P(x0)
3P(y0)=E 1, 2
4P(x0)→P(y0)→I 2–3
5x0=y0→(P(x0)→P(y0))→I 1–4
6∀y(x0=y→(P(x0)→P(y)))∀I 1–5
7∀x∀y(x=y→(P(x)→P(y)))∀I 1–6

The two ∀I lines cite the flagged boxes as 1–5 and 1–6: each flagged box immediately contains another box, so its range starts at that box’s first line (the convention of Section 4.4). At line 6 the name y0 appears in no premise (there are none), in no open assumption (the boxes on lines 1 and 2 have closed), and not in the conclusion; at line 7 the same holds for x0. The derivation has 7 lines.

The claim is one of the classical “axioms of equality”, often taken as a starting point in place of =E. Here it is a consequence. Conversely, with the claim as a premise, ∀E twice and →E twice would do the work of =E for the formula P(x); the rule does it for every formula at once.

4.7.4. Calculations are chains of substitutions

A calculation in a proof looks like this:

a+b=2⋅b+b=2⋅3+3=9,

written under the premises a=2⋅b and b=3. The chain is a single statement to the eye, but logically it is several equations, each obtained from the last. Here is the derivation it abbreviates, with one line of arithmetic, justified “arith” as in Section 4.3.

A chain as a derivation. From b=3 and a=2⋅b, derive a+b=9.

1b=3
2a=2⋅b
3a+b=a+b=I
4a+b=2⋅b+b=E 2, 3
5a+b=2⋅3+3=E 1, 4
62⋅3+3=9arith
7a+b=9=E 6, 5

The choices of φ, with z a variable not occurring in the terms:

  • line 4: φ=(a+b=z+b), rewriting the a on the right of line 3 and keeping the one on the left;
  • line 5: φ=(a+b=2⋅z+z), rewriting both remaining b’s on the right at once;
  • line 7: φ=(a+b=z), rewriting the whole right-hand side by the equation of line 6.

The pattern is general. A chain t1=t2=⋯=tn starts with t1=t1 by =I, keeps t1 fixed on the left, and rewrites the right-hand side once per link, each time by =E with the equation that justifies the link. Each link is either a premise, as on lines 4 and 5, or an arithmetic fact, as on line 7. The last line is t1=tn. Transitivity (Proposition 4.7.1 (b)) is the same move made once; a chain makes it n−1 times.

A mixed chain, such as a2+1=10≤10+b2 with a=3, is not made of =E alone. Its = links are =E steps as above, and a ≤ link needs a fact about ≤: here that b2≥0, so that adding b2 does not decrease a number. The = link before it then carries over by one more =E, with φ=(z≤10+b2) and the equation a2+1=10 turned round by symmetry (Proposition 4.7.1 (a)); transitivity of ≤ is needed only where two ≤ links meet, as in x≤y≤z. Those are facts about order, not about equality. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 derives them from the axioms of an ordered field; until then they enter derivations as “arith” lines, one per link.

Quick check. Line 5 of the chain rewrites both b’s on the right of line 4 at once. Which φ would rewrite only the b inside 2⋅b, and what line would it give? How would the chain then reach line 5?

Solution. Take φ=(a+b=2⋅z+b). Then line 4 is φ[b/z], and =E 1, 4 gives φ[3/z], the line a+b=2⋅3+b. One more =E with the same equation b=3 and φ=(a+b=2⋅3+z) then gives a+b=2⋅3+3, which is line 5. Marking both occurrences at once saves that line.

4.7.5. What equality sounds like in a proof

In a written proof, =E is the word “substituting”, or no word at all: the chain a+b=2b+b=9 is read as a sequence of substitutions, and the reader supplies the φ of each link. “By symmetry” or “rewriting the equation as t=s” is Proposition 4.7.1 (a). “Applying f to both sides”, “squaring both sides”, “adding c to both sides” are the congruence derivation above. And =I is almost never written, because t=t goes without saying; it is visible only in the first line of a formal chain, and in a proof assistant, where rfl proves t=t.

Here is a proof from school algebra, read link by link.

Claim. If a+b=0 and a+c=0, then b=c.

Proof. b=b+0=b+(a+c)=(b+a)+c=(a+b)+c=0+c=c.

The first link is the fact y+0=y for every y, applied at y=b (an instance by ∀E) and read from right to left: the chain needs b=b+0, which is the instance b+0=b turned round by symmetry. The second link rewrites the 0 by the premise a+c=0, again turned round, since the chain needs 0 to become a+c. The third and fourth are instances of associativity and commutativity. The fifth rewrites a+b by the premise a+b=0 in the direction written. The last is the instance 0+c=c. So the claim says that a number has at most one additive inverse; the facts it uses are the field axioms, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states as axioms and which here are school algebra.

4.7.6. Unique existence

Mathematics says “the limit of the sequence”, “the supremum of A”, “the additive inverse of a”. Each “the” makes two claims. There is such an object, and there is only one, so that the name picks it out. The second claim is the one that is easy to forget, and the one the claim above was about.

“There is exactly one x with φ”: there is one, and any other is it.

Definition 4.7.2 (Unique Existence)

Let φ be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in φ (Section 4.2). Then ∃!xφabbreviates∃x(φ∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x)). We read ∃!xφ as “there is exactly one x such that φ”, or “there is a unique x with φ”.

In words: there is an x that satisfies φ, and every y that satisfies φ (that is, satisfies φ with y in place of x) is equal to that x. The first conjunct is existence. The second is uniqueness, and it is a statement about the x already found: any other candidate coincides with it. Like the bounded quantifiers of Definition 4.1.1, ∃! is not a new symbol of the language but shorthand, and every rule applies to the formula it abbreviates.

Well-definedness. The abbreviation seems to depend on the choice of y. It does not, up to renaming a bound variable (Section 4.2). The argument rests on one fact about substitution, used again below: if y does not appear in φ, then replacing x by y and then y by a term t is the same as replacing x by t, that is, (φ[y/x])[t/y] is φ[t/x]. This is a structural induction on φ of the kind in Section 4.2. In a term, the y’s of s[y/x] are exactly the former x’s, so (s[y/x])[t/y]=s[t/x]; atomic formulas, ⊥ and the connectives follow clause by clause. For ∀xψ, both sides are ∀xψ, since substitution for x stops at ∀x and y does not appear in ψ (the second fact of Section 4.2). For ∀zψ with z not x, also z is not y, because y does not appear in φ; so both substitutions pass under the quantifier and the induction hypothesis applies, and ∃ is the same. Now let y and y′ be two admissible choices. If they are the same variable there is nothing to show. Otherwise y′ does not appear in φ[y/x]→y=x, since it is neither x nor y and does not appear in φ; so the bound y of ∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x) may be renamed y′, which gives ∀y′((φ[y/x])[y′/y]→y′=x). By the fact with t=y′, this is ∀y′(φ[y′/x]→y′=x), the formula written with y′.

Why y must not appear in φ. The condition keeps the new quantifier ∀y from capturing anything of φ’s own. Take φ=(x≤y), in which y is free, and read over N with y naming 0. “There is exactly one natural number x with x≤0” is true: x=0. The formula written with the forbidden bound variable y is ∃x(x≤y∧∀y(y≤y→y=x)), because (x≤y)[y/x] is y≤y. Its second conjunct says that every natural number equals x, which is false. The free y of φ, which was to name 0, has been captured by ∀y. With an admissible variable, say z, the formula is ∃x(x≤y∧∀z(z≤y→z=x)), which is true.

Examples. Simplest first; each is read over the domain named, with the informal truth of Section 4.1.

  1. Over R, ∃!x(x+2=5) is true. Existence: 3+2=5. Uniqueness: if y+2=5, then subtracting 2 gives y=3, so y is the x already found.
  2. Over N, ∃!x(x⋅x=4) is true. Existence: 2⋅2=4. Uniqueness: for a natural number y, if y≤1 then y⋅y≤1, and if y≥3 then y⋅y≥9; so y⋅y=4 forces y=2.
  3. Over R, ∃!x∀y(x+y=y) is true: 0 is the unique additive identity. Existence: 0+y=y for every y. Uniqueness: suppose z+y=y for every y. Apply this to the one instance y=0 (by ∀E): z+0=0. Since also z+0=z, symmetry and transitivity give z=0. The whole uniqueness proof is the choice of the instance y=0.
  4. Degenerate. For any constant c, ∃!x(x=c) holds in every domain, and it is derivable from no premises (the derivation follows). By contrast, ∃!x(x=x) says that the domain has exactly one element, which is false in N, Z and R: existence holds and uniqueness fails.

Nonexample by minimal change. Keep example 2 and change the domain to Z. Existence still holds, with the same witness 2. Uniqueness fails: y=−2 also satisfies y⋅y=4, and −2≠2. So over Z, ∃!x(x⋅x=4) is false, and the failing clause is exactly the second conjunct.

The derivation of ∃!x(x=c), with the abbreviation written out, shows that ∃! needs no rules of its own:

1c=c=I
2y0y0=c
3y0=c→y0=c→I 2–2
4∀y(y=c→y=c)∀I 2–3
5c=c∧∀y(y=c→y=c)∧I 1, 4
6∃x(x=c∧∀y(y=c→y=x))∃I 5

Line 3 closes a box whose only line is its assumption: the box shows y0=c→y0=c, as P→P is shown in Chapter 1. Line 6 is ∃I with the witness c, and it reads line 5 as ψ[c/x] for ψ=(x=c∧∀y(y=c→y=x)), which marks with x the first c and the last one, and keeps the other two. The choice of which occurrences to mark is the one discussed with Definition 4.5.1.

Warning. Uniqueness is not existence. A uniqueness argument (“suppose y also satisfies φ; then y=x”) proves nothing about whether anything satisfies φ. Over R, every two solutions of x2=−1 are equal, vacuously, because there are none; yet no real number is “the” square root of −1. Conversely, an existence proof does not give uniqueness: x2=1 has the solution 1, and “the solution” would be wrong, since −1 is another. Before writing “the”, check both halves.

4.7.7. How uniqueness is used and proved

A proof of “exactly one” rarely follows the shape of Definition 4.7.2, which ties the uniqueness clause to the witness just found. It proves two separate statements: there is at least one, and there is at most one. The second is “any two objects with the property are equal”, and it makes no mention of a witness. The next result says that the two shapes say the same thing.

Proposition 4.7.2 (Two Halves of Unique Existence)

Let φ be a formula, x a variable, and y a variable other than x that does not appear in φ. Then ∃!xφ⊣⊢∃xφ∧∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y).

The right-hand side is “existence and at most one”. Its second conjunct is what a mathematician proves under the heading “uniqueness”: take two objects x and y with the property, and show x=y.

Idea. Both directions are searches in the style of Section 2.6 with the quantifier steps. For ⊢, the premise is an ∃, so open its ∃E box first, with a witness x0: inside it, φ[x0/x] gives existence at once by ∃I, and “at most one” is a ∀∀ goal, which opens two flagged boxes u0, v0. Two objects u0, v0 with the property are each equal to the witness x0, by the uniqueness clause, and so equal to each other: the witness is the “third point” that links them. For ⊣, open the ∃E box on ∃xφ with a witness x0; the goal inside is ∃!xφ, whose witness will be x0 again, and the uniqueness clause for x0 comes from “at most one” applied to the pair x0, y0.

Proof. Choose four distinct variables x0, u0, v0, y0 that do not appear in φ, and none of which is x or y. Three facts about substitution are used throughout. First, since y does not appear in φ, (φ[y/x])[t/y] is φ[t/x] for every term t, the fact proved for the well-definedness of Definition 4.7.2. Second, φ[y/x] has no free x (every free x became y), so it is unchanged by a substitution for x. Third, for a term t that does not contain y, φ[t/x] contains no y, so it is unchanged by a substitution for y.

(⊢) The following is a derivation with premise ∃!xφ, written out.

1∃x(φ∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x))
2x0φ[x0/x]∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x0)
3φ[x0/x]∧E 2
4∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x0)∧E 2
5∃xφ∃I 3
6u0v0φ[u0/x]∧φ[v0/x]
7φ[u0/x]∧E 6
8φ[v0/x]∧E 6
9φ[u0/x]→u0=x0∀E 4
10u0=x0→E 9, 7
11φ[v0/x]→v0=x0∀E 4
12v0=x0→E 11, 8
13v0=v0=I
14x0=v0=E 12, 13
15u0=v0=E 14, 10
16φ[u0/x]∧φ[v0/x]→u0=v0→I 6–15
17∀y(φ[u0/x]∧φ[y/x]→u0=y)∀I 6–16
18∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y)∀I 6–17
19∃xφ∧∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y)∧I 5, 18
20∃xφ∧∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y)∃E 1, 2–19

Lines 9 and 11 are ∀E on line 4 at u0 and at v0, by the first substitution fact; each term is a variable not bound in φ[y/x]→y=x0, so it is free for y there. Lines 13 and 14 are the symmetry of Proposition 4.7.1 (a), written out; line 15 is =E with the equation x0=v0 and ψ=(u0=z), which turns line 10 into u0=v0. Line 17 is ∀I with the flag v0: line 16 is its instance at v0 (by the third and first substitution facts), and v0 appears in no premise, in no assumption still open at line 17 (only line 2 is, and v0 is not in it), and not in line 17. Line 18 is ∀I with the flag u0 in the same way; its instance at u0 is line 17, by the second substitution fact. Finally, line 20 closes the ∃E box: its last line 19 does not contain x0, and x0 is in neither line 1 nor any open assumption.

(⊣) The following is a derivation with the right-hand side as premise.

1∃xφ∧∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y)
2∃xφ∧E 1
3∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y)∧E 1
4x0φ[x0/x]
5y0φ[y0/x]
6∀y(φ[x0/x]∧φ[y/x]→x0=y)∀E 3
7φ[x0/x]∧φ[y0/x]→x0=y0∀E 6
8φ[x0/x]∧φ[y0/x]∧I 4, 5
9x0=y0→E 7, 8
10x0=x0=I
11y0=x0=E 9, 10
12φ[y0/x]→y0=x0→I 5–11
13∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x0)∀I 5–12
14φ[x0/x]∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x0)∧I 4, 13
15∃x(φ∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x))∃I 14
16∃x(φ∧∀y(φ[y/x]→y=x))∃E 2, 4–15

Line 6 is ∀E at x0 on line 3, by the second substitution fact, and line 7 is ∀E at y0 on line 6, by the third and first. Lines 10 and 11 are symmetry, written out. Line 13 is ∀I with the flag y0: line 12 is its instance at y0, by the first substitution fact; at line 13 the open assumptions are line 4, which does not contain y0, the premise does not contain it either, and neither does line 13. Line 15 is ∃I with the witness x0, which is free for x since it does not appear in φ; line 14 is its instance at x0, by the second substitution fact. Line 16 closes the ∃E box: line 15 does not contain x0, and x0 is in neither line 2 nor the premise, which is the only assumption open outside the box. This proves both directions.

In practice this is how “there is exactly one” is proved: an existence proof, then a separate “suppose x and y both satisfy φ; then x=y”. And it is how it is used: from ∃!xφ we may take a witness, and we may identify any two objects with the property. The claim about additive inverses above was the “at most one” half; existence of an inverse is a field axiom.

One more instance: “the maximum”. A maximum of a set A of reals is an element m∈A with a≤m for every a∈A. If m and m′ are both maxima, then m′≤m (apply the property of m to the element m′∈A) and m≤m′ (apply the property of m′ to m∈A), so m=m′ by the order fact that a≤b and b≤a give a=b. That is “at most one”; a set may have no maximum at all, such as (0,1), so existence is a separate question. Only when both halves are known may we write “the maximum of A”.

4.7.8. The search method: one more step

Each of Sections 4.3 to 4.6 added a step to the search method of Section 2.6. Equality adds one.

  • An equation. When an equation t1=t2 is available and the goal differs from an available line only in some occurrences of t1 and t2, look for the φ that makes one =E turn the line into the goal: mark with x exactly the places where they differ. If the equation points the wrong way, turn it round first (sym). If no available line will do, make one with =I, as the proof of Proposition 4.7.1 did.

Section 4.8 collects all the steps into one method.

4.7.9. The rule, phrase and Lean table, completed

Chapter 1 began a table that pairs each rule with the sentence that performs it in a written proof and, for readers who use a proof assistant, with the Lean code that does the same (Sections 1.3–1.7), and Chapter 2 added the rows for negation, the biconditional, and the classical rules (Sections 2.1–2.5). Sections 4.3–4.6 added a row for each quantifier rule, and this section adds the two rows for equality. Here is the whole table for the calculus of this volume. Nothing later depends on the last column, and Chapter 5 turns the middle column into a full dictionary of proof phrases.

Rule You write Lean
∧I “We show P, and we show Q.” constructor
∧E “In particular, P.” h.1 (and h.2)
→E “Since P implies Q, and P holds, Q.” exact h hp
→I “Assume P. … Hence Q.” intro hp
R “As shown above, P.” exact hp
∨I “So P or Q holds.” left (or Or.inl hp); right
∨E “Case 1: P. … so R. Case 2: Q. … so R. In either case, R.” Or.elim h (or cases h)
¬E “…, which contradicts …” exact hn hp (goal False)
⊥E “This case cannot occur.” “So there is nothing to prove.” exfalso
¬I “Suppose φ. … This is a contradiction. Hence not φ.” intro hp (goal False)
↔I “(⇒) Suppose P. … so Q. (⇐) Suppose Q. … so P.” constructor
↔E “Since P holds if and only if Q does, and P holds, so does Q.” h.mp hp / h.mpr hq
RAA “Suppose, for a contradiction, that φ fails. … This is impossible. Hence φ.” by_contra h
∀E “In particular, for x=t, …”; “applying the hypothesis to t, …” h t (or specialize h t)
∀I “Let x be arbitrary. … Since x was arbitrary, …” intro x
∃I “Take x=t. Then …” use t (or Exists.intro t h)
∃E “Choose x with … . Then …” obtain (or Exists.elim h)
=I (usually unwritten) “t=t.” rfl
=E “Substituting t2 for t1, …”; a chain t1=t2=⋯=tn rw [h]; chains calc

Of the derived rules of Chapter 2, MT, CP and DS have their rows in Section 2.3, and ¬¬E and LEM in Section 2.5; all the derived sequents are collected in Section 2.6. With the two equality rows, every rule of the calculus has its phrase.

4.7.10. Exercises

A. Check your understanding

Exercise (A1)

  • (a) State =I and =E as schemas, with the side condition of =E.

  • (b) In the derivation below, name for each of lines 4, 5, 6, and 8 the rule, the cited lines, and the formula φ (with a variable z as its hole).

    1a=b+1
    2b=2
    3a⋅a=a⋅a=I
    4a⋅a=(b+1)⋅a=E 1, 3
    5a⋅a=(b+1)⋅(b+1)=E 1, 4
    6a⋅a=(2+1)⋅(2+1)=E 2, 5
    7(2+1)⋅(2+1)=9arith
    8a⋅a=9=E 7, 6

  • (c) In the same derivation, could lines 4 and 5 be replaced by one line? With which φ?

  • (d) True or false, with a reason: from the lines a=b and P(b), one application of =E gives P(a).

  • (e) Write ∃!x(x⋅x=9) without the symbol ∃!, and decide whether it is true over N and over Z.

Solution. (a) =I: at any line k, write t=t, for any term t, citing nothing. =E: from t1=t2 on line i and φ[t1/x] on line j, both available at line k, write φ[t2/x] on line k; side condition: t1 and t2 are both free for x in φ.

(b) Line 4: =E 1, 3, with φ=(a⋅a=z⋅a), which rewrites the first a on the right. Line 5: =E 1, 4, with φ=(a⋅a=(b+1)⋅z). Line 6: =E 2, 5, with φ=(a⋅a=(z+1)⋅(z+1)), which rewrites both b’s at once. Line 8: =E 7, 6, with φ=(a⋅a=z). In each case the left-hand side a⋅a is written out in φ, so it is kept.

(c) Yes: =E 1, 3 with φ=(a⋅a=z⋅z) gives a⋅a=(b+1)⋅(b+1) in one step, rewriting both a’s on the right and keeping the two on the left.

(d) False. With the equation a=b, =E passes from φ[a/x] to φ[b/x]. The line P(b) is φ[b/x] for φ=P(x), so the rule would need the equation b=a. One application of symmetry first (Proposition 4.7.1 (a)) gives b=a, and then =E gives P(a).

(e) ∃x(x⋅x=9∧∀y(y⋅y=9→y=x)). Over N it is true: x=3 works, and a natural number y with y⋅y=9 is 3, since y≤2 gives y⋅y≤4 and y≥4 gives y⋅y≥16. Over Z it is false: whatever x is proposed, 3 and −3 both satisfy y⋅y=9, and they cannot both equal x.

B. Practice

Exercise (B1: The identity is unique)

A set with an operation ⋅ has an identity e if e⋅x=x and x⋅e=x for every x. Derive ∀x(e⋅x=x∧x⋅e=x),∀x(e′⋅x=x∧x⋅e′=x)⊢e=e′, where e and e′ are constants. Which half of “there is exactly one identity” does this prove?

Hint: look at the one element that both premises can say something about.

Solution. The goal is an equation between e and e′, and the only term that both premises can connect to both is the product e⋅e′. Instantiate the first premise at e′ and the second at e (∀E, reading the terms off the goal):

1∀x(e⋅x=x∧x⋅e=x)
2∀x(e′⋅x=x∧x⋅e′=x)
3e⋅e′=e′∧e′⋅e=e′∀E 1
4e⋅e′=e′∧E 3
5e′⋅e=e∧e⋅e′=e∀E 2
6e⋅e′=e∧E 5
7e=e′=E 6, 4

Line 7 uses the equation e⋅e′=e of line 6 to rewrite the left side of line 4, with φ=(z=e′): φ[e⋅e′/z] is line 4, and φ[e/z] is e=e′. In prose: e=e⋅e′=e′, the first equation because e′ is an identity and the second because e is.

This is the “at most one” half: any two identities are equal. It says nothing about whether an identity exists. To use it in Proposition 4.7.2, take φ=∀z(x⋅z=z∧z⋅x=z), and run lines 3–7 again with variables u0, v0 in place of e, e′: inside flagged boxes for u0 and v0 and a →I box on φ[u0/x]∧φ[v0/x], the two premises (with z as their bound variable) come from that assumption by ∧E, and the same steps give u0=v0. Then →I and ∀I twice give ∀x∀y(φ∧φ[y/x]→x=y), the second conjunct of the proposition. With the existence of one identity as well, Proposition 4.7.2 gives “there is exactly one”.

Exercise (B2: A unique square root of zero)

Over R, write ∃!x(x⋅x=0) without ∃!, and prove it: existence, then uniqueness in the form “suppose y also satisfies …”.

Hint: a product of two nonzero reals is nonzero.

Solution. Written out, the statement is ∃x(x⋅x=0∧∀y(y⋅y=0→y=x)). We take the witness x=0 and prove the two conjuncts.

Existence. 0⋅0=0.

Uniqueness. Let y be a real number, and suppose y⋅y=0. If y≠0, then y⋅y is a product of two nonzero reals and so is nonzero, which contradicts y⋅y=0. Hence y=0, which is the witness. Since y was arbitrary, every y with y⋅y=0 equals 0.

So 0 witnesses the existential, and ∃!x(x⋅x=0) holds. The rules behind the words: “we take the witness x=0” is ∃I, postponed to the end as usual; “let y be a real number” is a flagged box for ∀I; “suppose y⋅y=0” is a →I box; “if y≠0 … contradicts” is an RAA box on y≠0. (That box gives y=0 directly; ¬I would give only ¬(y≠0). Since for reals y=0 or y≠0 is also a school fact, a proof by cases would do as well.)

Exercise (B3: Exactly one fixed point)

A fixed point of a function f:R→R is a real x with f(x)=x.

  • (a) Formalize “f has exactly one fixed point” over R, first with ∃! and then without it.
  • (b) Write a formula without ∃! that says “f does not have exactly one fixed point”, in the form “there is none, or there are two different ones”.
  • (c) Decide the statement of (a) for f(x)=x⋅x, for f(x)=x+1 and for f(x)=2⋅x, and check your answer against the formula of (b).

Solution. (a) With ∃!: ∃!x(f(x)=x). Written out, with y as the new variable: ∃x(f(x)=x∧∀y(f(y)=y→y=x)).

(b) ¬∃x(f(x)=x)∨∃x∃y(f(x)=x∧f(y)=y∧x≠y). Read informally over R: either no real number is fixed, or two different ones are. That is exactly the failure of “exactly one”. If no x is fixed, the first disjunct holds. If some x is fixed but the uniqueness clause fails for it, then some y is fixed and differs from x. Conversely, either disjunct rules out a unique fixed point: with none there is no witness, and two different fixed points x≠y would both have to equal any proposed witness w, giving x=y. (Section 4.9 derives such negations mechanically, one quantifier at a time.)

(c) For f(x)=x⋅x: x⋅x=x holds for x=0 and for x=1, so there are two different fixed points; (a) is false, and the second disjunct of (b) is true with x=0, y=1. For f(x)=x+1: x+1=x has no solution, so (a) is false and the first disjunct of (b) is true. For f(x)=2⋅x: 2x=x gives x=0, and 0 is fixed; so (a) is true with the witness 0, and both disjuncts of (b) are false.

C. Going deeper

Exercise (C1: Two unique quantifiers do not commute)

Show that ∃!x∃!yR(x,y) and ∃!y∃!xR(x,y) can have different truth values, by giving a finite domain D and a two-place relation R on it for which the first is true and the second false. Check both, reading ∃! informally.

Hint: first say in words what each sentence claims about the rows and columns of a table of R.

Solution. What any answer must satisfy. Call x single if exactly one y has R(x,y), and call y co-single if exactly one x has R(x,y). The first sentence says that exactly one element is single. The second says that exactly one element is co-single. So an answer needs exactly one single element and a number of co-single elements other than one: none, or two or more.

An example. Take D={0,1,2} and R={(1,2),(2,0),(2,1)}.

  • Single elements: 0 has no partner, 1 has exactly one (2), and 2 has two (0 and 1). So 1 is the only single element, and ∃!x∃!yR(x,y) is true, with the witness 1.
  • Co-single elements: y=0 is reached only from x=2; y=1 only from x=2; y=2 only from x=1. All three are co-single, so there is not exactly one, and ∃!y∃!xR(x,y) is false.

No example exists on one or two elements (there are only 2+16=18 relations on such domains). On one element, 0 is single and co-single exactly when R(0,0) holds, so the two sentences agree. On two elements, suppose exactly one element is single; after relabeling, call it 0, and let c be its only partner. Then 1 is not single, so it has no partners or two. If it has none, column c has one entry and the other column has none. If it has two, column c has two entries and the other column has one. Either way exactly one element is co-single. Exchanging the roles of rows and columns gives the converse, so the two sentences have the same truth value. Three elements is therefore the smallest possible domain.

The moral: ∃! is not a quantifier that commutes with its own kind, as two ∃’s do. “Exactly one” hides a ∀ (the uniqueness clause), and the order of a ∀ and an ∃ matters.

Exercise (C2: “At most one”, two ways)

Let P be a one-place predicate symbol. Derive both directions of ∀x∀y(P(x)∧P(y)→x=y)⊣⊢¬∃x∃y((P(x)∧P(y))∧x≠y), and say which of your two derivations uses RAA, and at which line.

Solution (Hint 1). The right-hand side is a negation: for ⊢, open a ¬I box, and inside it two ∃E boxes. For ⊣, the goal is ∀∀, then an implication, then an equation.

Solution (Hint 2). In the ⊣ direction, open flagged boxes for x0 and y0 and a →I box on P(x0)∧P(y0). The goal is now the atomic formula x0=y0. Which resources can give it?

Solution. (⊢) The goal is a negation, so a ¬I box opens on ∃x∃y(…); inside, the premise-directed step opens an ∃E box for each ∃, with the goal ⊥ as each box’s last line. The premise, instantiated at the two witnesses, gives x0=y0, which clashes with x0≠y0.

1∀x∀y(P(x)∧P(y)→x=y)
2∃x∃y((P(x)∧P(y))∧x≠y)
3x0∃y((P(x0)∧P(y))∧x0≠y)
4y0(P(x0)∧P(y0))∧x0≠y0
5P(x0)∧P(y0)∧E 4
6x0≠y0∧E 4
7∀y(P(x0)∧P(y)→x0=y)∀E 1
8P(x0)∧P(y0)→x0=y0∀E 7
9x0=y0→E 8, 5
10⊥¬E 9, 6
11⊥∃E 3, 4–10
12⊥∃E 2, 3–11
13¬∃x∃y((P(x)∧P(y))∧x≠y)¬I 2–12

The brackets in the statement are written out because the default groups a longer conjunction to the right (Section 3.4); with the grouping (P(x0)∧P(y0))∧x0≠y0 on line 4, ∧E takes out its two halves on lines 5 and 6. At line 11, y0 is not in ⊥, not in line 3, not in the premise, and not in the assumptions still open (lines 2 and 3). At line 12 the same holds for x0, with line 2 the only open assumption.

(⊣) The goal-directed steps open flagged boxes for x0 and y0 and a →I box on P(x0)∧P(y0), leaving the goal x0=y0. No resource gives an equation, so the search is stuck, and step 5 of the method applies: an RAA box on x0≠y0. Inside, ∧I and two ∃I steps rebuild the formula that the premise denies.

1¬∃x∃y((P(x)∧P(y))∧x≠y)
2x0y0P(x0)∧P(y0)
3x0≠y0
4(P(x0)∧P(y0))∧x0≠y0∧I 2, 3
5∃y((P(x0)∧P(y))∧x0≠y)∃I 4
6∃x∃y((P(x)∧P(y))∧x≠y)∃I 5
7⊥¬E 6, 1
8x0=y0RAA 3–7
9P(x0)∧P(y0)→x0=y0→I 2–8
10∀y(P(x0)∧P(y)→x0=y)∀I 2–9
11∀x∀y(P(x)∧P(y)→x=y)∀I 2–10

The ⊣ derivation uses RAA, at line 8: the box opens with x0≠y0, that is ¬(x0=y0), and closes with x0=y0. Closing it by ¬I instead would give ¬¬(x0=y0), and no rule of Chapter 1 or Sections 2.1–2.4 removes the double negation. (With the derived rule ¬¬E of Section 2.5, that ¬I box followed by ¬¬E is an equally good derivation; its classical step is the ¬¬E line, which hides an RAA.) The ⊢ derivation uses no classical rule.

Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: ⊢: opens a ¬I box on the existential, with the goal ⊥. - 2: ⊢: two ∃E boxes with fresh witnesses, each ending in ⊥, and the premise instantiated at those witnesses. - 2: ⊣: two flagged boxes and a →I box, in the order read off the goal. - 2: ⊣: an RAA box on x0≠y0, with the clash obtained by ∧I and two ∃I steps. - 2: names the ⊣ direction as the one using RAA, and the line. - A ¬I box on x0≠y0 followed by ¬¬E, or an LEM split on x0=y0 whose second case reaches ⊥ the same way (then ⊥E), earns the 2 points of the RAA-box line; for the naming line, the reader names the ¬¬E or LEM line as the classical step, a derived rule whose derivation uses RAA (Section 2.5). Fatal errors (0 for the step): an ∃E box closing on a line that contains its witness; a ∀I over a name in an open assumption; ¬I claimed to give x0=y0.
